articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian and Cuban Entities, Issues New General Licenses and FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026. This action also included the issuance of new and amended General Licenses (GLs) and Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) to provide guidance on the updated sanctions.

The designations targeted 16 individuals and 11 entities linked to Iran, including financial institutions, currency exchange firms, and energy and trading companies. Notably, Cuba's Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA) was designated due to its alleged ties with Iran's Karafarin Bank, which has been under sanctions since 2020.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that 'Communist Cuba has been allowed to operate as an outpost for malign actors and terror groups — including the Islamic Republic of Iran, the world's number one state sponsor of terrorism — to target the United States.' Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez, however, described the action as 'aggressive,' asserting that BICSA is an 'absolutely legitimate bank whose transactions in Cuba and around the world are also absolutely legitimate.'

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-related Designation
body: On October 14, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a Venezuela-related designation removal. This action indicates a specific entity or individual previously sanctioned under the Venezuela program has been delisted.

Such removals typically occur when the designated party meets the criteria for delisting, such as a change in circumstances or a demonstration of compliance with U.S. sanctions policy. The specific details of the removed designation were not immediately provided in the announcement.

This action follows previous OFAC guidance related to Venezuela, which has included general licenses authorizing certain transactions in the telecommunications sector, though explicitly excluding transactions involving sanctioned entities from countries like Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba, or China.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions aim to disrupt illicit financial networks that support drug trafficking and terrorist organizations globally.

These designations fall under OFAC's broader efforts to combat transnational criminal organizations and terrorist financing, which are critical components of U.S. national security. The specific individuals and entities designated were not detailed in the initial announcement but are now subject to asset blocking and other restrictions.

Such designations underscore the ongoing commitment of the U.S. Treasury to leverage its sanctions authorities against those who threaten international stability and security through illicit activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-related General License
body: On October 9, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License. This license authorizes specific transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the extensive sanctions program targeting Russia.

General Licenses are frequently used by OFAC to carve out exceptions for certain activities, ensuring that sanctions do not unduly impact humanitarian efforts, legitimate trade, or other policy objectives. The specifics of this new license aim to facilitate particular types of transactions while maintaining the overall pressure on the Russian economy.

This action follows previous updates to Russia sanctions regulations, including additional SDN designations targeting Russian financial intermediaries and energy sector entities, and the extension of EU sanctions related to actions threatening Ukraine's sovereignty.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-related Designations and Issues Amended Russia-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026, alongside the issuance of an Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License. These actions reflect the U.S. government's ongoing strategy to exert pressure on Iran while also refining its approach to Russia sanctions.

The Iran-related designations target entities and individuals deemed to be supporting activities contrary to U.S. national security interests, with nearly half of recently designated entities, all based in China, supporting Chinese military modernization and sanctioned parties in Iran.

The amended Russia-related General License indicates a recalibration of existing restrictions, likely to address specific operational or humanitarian concerns, while the new Iran-related General License may permit certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Alert on Iran Sanctions, Amends FAQ, and Announces Designations Removals
body: On October 5, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) published an alert warning foreign financial institutions (FFIs) that they could be targeted at any time without advance notification for transacting with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions.

Concurrently, OFAC amended Iran-related FAQ 156, removing language that previously indicated the Treasury Department would generally contact FFIs before making a finding of sanctionable activity. This change signals a more aggressive enforcement posture.

The alert is part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' launched by OFAC on August 24, 2026, to cut off financial resources supporting the Iranian regime. FFIs providing services to Iranian banks or their subsidiaries risk sanctions for supporting sanctioned sectors of Iran's economy.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Global Sanctions and Export Controls Blog

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Terrorism Designations on October 2, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities identified as supporting terrorist activities globally, aiming to disrupt their financial and operational networks.

These actions are part of the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to combating terrorism financing and preventing designated individuals and groups from accessing the international financial system. The specific details of the designated parties were not immediately released.
Such designations typically result in the blocking of assets under U.S. jurisdiction and generally prohibit U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with the designated parties.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-related Designations and Updates, Transnational Criminal Organization Designation
body: On October 1, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and designations updates, along with a Transnational Criminal Organizations designation. This comprehensive action underscores the U.S. government's multi-pronged approach to countering threats from Iran and organized crime.

The Iran-related actions include the designation of additional entities and individuals, as well as updates to existing designations, further tightening the sanctions regime against the country. This follows a series of actions taken by OFAC in September 2026, including sanctions against Iran's aviation sector.

Additionally, OFAC published an Iran-related Determination and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question, providing further clarity and reinforcing the U.S. policy of economic pressure against the Iranian regime.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A., imposing a civil penalty of $11,662,930 for apparent violations of numerous U.S. sanctions programs. This penalty is part of a broader enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department.

Bank of America processed millions of dollars in payments in apparent violation of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism. OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious and largely not voluntarily self-disclosed.
The settlement amount reflects no reduction to the base penalty, including no mitigation for remedial measures or cooperation, underscoring OFAC's serious view of the bank's compliance failures.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has entered into a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), agreeing to pay $175,015. The settlement resolves alleged violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

Details of the specific violations were not immediately released but typically involve transactions with sanctioned entities, countries, or individuals. OFAC's enforcement actions aim to ensure compliance with U.S. foreign policy and national security objectives.

This settlement highlights the importance for logistics and shipping companies to maintain robust sanctions compliance programs to prevent inadvertent violations when facilitating international trade.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1,427,230 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has been assessed a civil penalty of $1,427,230 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for violations of U.S. sanctions regulations. This enforcement action underscores OFAC's commitment to holding individuals accountable for non-compliance.

While the specific nature of the violations was not detailed in the public notice, individual penalties often stem from direct involvement in prohibited transactions, such as facilitating payments to sanctioned entities or engaging in trade with embargoed countries.

This case serves as a reminder that sanctions compliance obligations extend beyond corporate entities to individuals, who can face significant financial repercussions for breaches of OFAC regulations.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Pays $60,764 to Settle OFAC Violations
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle its civil liability for apparent violations of sanctions regulations administered by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The settlement resolves allegations of non-compliance with U.S. sanctions laws.

The specific violations were not publicly detailed but likely involved transactions with sanctioned jurisdictions or entities. Companies in various sectors, including manufacturing and technology, are subject to OFAC regulations and must ensure their global operations comply with U.S. sanctions.

This enforcement action highlights the need for companies to implement robust compliance programs, including thorough screening of customers and transactions, to prevent engaging in prohibited activities.

articles.headline: Iran's President Calls for Global Attention to Environmental Impact of Military Conflicts
body: Iran's President Pezeshkian has called on the world to pay more serious attention to the environmental impacts of military conflicts. This statement comes amidst ongoing regional tensions and conflicts, which often have severe and long-lasting ecological consequences.

The president's remarks highlight a growing concern among some nations regarding the broader, often overlooked, damage inflicted by warfare beyond immediate casualties and infrastructure destruction. Environmental degradation from conflict can include pollution, resource depletion, and ecosystem destruction.

This appeal aligns with broader international discussions about climate change and environmental protection, urging a more holistic view of conflict resolution that considers ecological sustainability.

articles.headline: Poland Scrambles Fighter Jets as Russia Strikes Western Ukraine
body: Poland scrambled fighter jets as Russia launched strikes on western Ukraine, raising concerns among countries along NATO's eastern flank about the risk of escalation in the ongoing conflict. This action underscores the heightened tensions and the potential for spillover effects into neighboring territories.

The repeated Russian strikes on Ukrainian targets, particularly in regions closer to NATO borders, have prompted defensive measures and increased vigilance from alliance members. Such incidents highlight the precarious security situation in Eastern Europe.

NATO countries have consistently expressed concerns about the territorial integrity of Ukraine and the broader implications of the conflict for regional stability, leading to enhanced military readiness and support for Ukraine.

The attack on a key government facility underscores the Houthis' continued military capabilities and their willingness to target high-value objectives. This action is likely to further destabilize the already fragile security situation in Yemen.
The escalating conflict has drawn international condemnation and calls for de-escalation, as it continues to have devastating humanitarian consequences for the Yemeni population.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty on Bank of America for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., for widespread and egregious violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and its implementing regulations. This represents the largest civil money penalty in OCC history.

The OCC found that Bank of America's BSA/AML compliance program was deficient and ineffective, with a transaction monitoring system that failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions. This resulted in the bank filing a large number of late suspicious activity reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars, many with indicia of money laundering.

Despite a December 2024 cease-and-desist order requiring the bank to address its BSA/AML deficiencies, Bank of America failed to prioritize compliance and did not complete many significant steps needed to establish an effective program. The OCC emphasized that the bank's poor response to its BSA deficiencies was unacceptable, threatening U.S. national and economic security.

articles.headline: OCC and Federal Reserve Issue Parallel Consent Orders for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System issued parallel consent orders on October 8, 2026, against a major financial services corporation and bank holding company. These orders address significant deficiencies in the institution's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) compliance, along with enterprise-wide financial crimes compliance programs.

The OCC found that the bank's BSA/AML program suffered from systemic internal-control gaps, weak independent testing, and inadequate BSA/AML training. Specifically, the bank's risk assessment focused too narrowly on its demand-deposit business, failing to adequately address risks associated with its much larger credit and charge-card business.

These coordinated actions highlight that material BSA/AML failures, particularly those related to deficient transaction monitoring and suspicious-activity reporting, continue to result in substantial monetary penalties and extensive remediation obligations for financial institutions.

articles.headline: BIS Adds Over Three Dozen Entities to Entity List, Primarily Targeting China
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) of the U.S. Department of Commerce announced the addition of more than three dozen companies to its Entity List, effective immediately. This marks the second round of restrictions imposed by the United States in as many weeks.

Out of the 37 entities added, 28 are from China, with others from Belarus, Burma, Pakistan, Russia, and Taiwan. Nearly half of the Chinese entities were cited for supporting Chinese military modernization and sanctioned parties in Iran.

BIS also added a significant number of Chinese and Pakistani entities for supporting ballistic missile and unsafeguarded nuclear activities, and several entities in Russia, Belarus, and one in Taiwan for supporting Russia's military.
articles.source: U.S. Department of Commerce BIS / Legal 500

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
